title: Encapsulation and Access Modifiers
prompt: Explain the concept of encapsulation in object-oriented programming and describe how access modifiers support it.
reference_answer: Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data and the methods that operate on that data within a single unit, typically a class, while restricting direct access to some of the object's components. Access modifiers such as private, protected, and public control the visibility of fields and methods, enforcing information hiding. By making fields private and exposing controlled access through getters and setters, a class can validate changes to its internal state and hide implementation details from the outside world. This reduces coupling between classes and makes code easier to maintain and refactor.

title: Inheritance vs Polymorphism
prompt: Compare inheritance and polymorphism in object-oriented programming, with examples.
reference_answer: Inheritance allows a class to acquire the fields and methods of another class, enabling code reuse through a parent-child relationship. Polymorphism allows objects of different classes to be treated through a common interface, most commonly via method overriding, so that the same method call can produce different behavior depending on the runtime type of the object. Abstract classes and interfaces often combine both concepts by defining a shared contract that subclasses implement in their own way.

title: Database Normalization
prompt: Explain database normalization and describe the goals of 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF.
reference_answer: Normalization is the process of organizing relational database tables to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity. First normal form (1NF) requires atomic column values, second normal form (2NF) removes partial dependencies on a composite key, and third normal form (3NF) removes transitive functional dependencies so non-key attributes depend only on the primary key. Applying these forms step by step prevents update, insert, and delete anomalies.

title: ACID Properties of Transactions
prompt: Describe the ACID properties of database transactions and why each one matters.
reference_answer: ACID properties describe the guarantees that a database transaction provides to keep data reliable: atomicity ensures a transaction fully completes or has no effect, consistency ensures the database moves between valid states, isolation ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other, and durability ensures committed changes survive system failures. Together these properties make transactions safe under concurrency and failure.

title: The OSI Model
prompt: Describe the OSI model and explain the role of at least three of its layers.
reference_answer: The OSI model divides network communication into seven layers, each responsible for a specific function, from the physical layer that transmits raw bits, through the network layer that routes packets using IP addresses, up to the application layer that provides services directly to end user software. The transport layer, using protocols like TCP, provides reliable delivery and flow control between endpoints. This layered design allows each layer to evolve independently.

title: TCP vs UDP
prompt: Compare TCP and UDP as transport-layer protocols, including their trade-offs.
reference_answer: TCP and UDP are both transport-layer protocols, but they make very different trade-offs between reliability and speed. TCP is connection-oriented, establishing a handshake and guaranteeing reliable, in-order delivery through acknowledgements and retransmission. UDP is connectionless and sends packets without delivery guarantees, resulting in lower latency that suits real-time applications such as video streaming and gaming.

title: Waterfall vs Agile
prompt: Compare the waterfall model and agile methodology as approaches to the software development lifecycle.
reference_answer: The waterfall model and agile methodology represent two very different approaches to organizing the software development lifecycle. Waterfall moves sequentially through fixed phases such as requirements, design, implementation, and testing, assuming requirements are well understood upfront. Agile breaks work into short iterations called sprints, delivering working software incrementally and adapting to feedback and changing requirements along the way.

title: Big-O Notation and Time Complexity
prompt: Explain Big-O notation and give examples of algorithms with different time complexities.
reference_answer: Big-O notation describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as the size of its input increases, typically focusing on worst-case analysis. A linear search runs in O(n) time because it may inspect every element, binary search on sorted data runs in O(log n) time, and a naive nested-loop comparison runs in O(n^2) time. Big-O allows algorithms to be compared independent of hardware or implementation details.

title: Quicksort vs Merge Sort
prompt: Compare quicksort and merge sort, including their approach, complexity, and stability.
reference_answer: Quicksort and merge sort are both efficient divide-and-conquer sorting algorithms. Quicksort selects a pivot and partitions elements around it, achieving O(n log n) average-case time but O(n^2) worst-case time on adversarial input. Merge sort always splits the array in half and merges sorted halves, giving guaranteed O(n log n) performance and stability, meaning equal elements retain their relative order.

title: Stack vs Queue
prompt: Compare the stack and queue data structures, including their ordering and typical uses.
reference_answer: A stack and a queue are both linear data structures, but they differ in the order in which elements are added and removed. A stack follows last-in-first-out (LIFO) order using push and pop operations, making it useful for function call tracking and undo operations. A queue follows first-in-first-out (FIFO) order using enqueue and dequeue operations, making it useful for task scheduling and breadth-first search.
